MINNEAPOLIS, Minnesota (CNN) -- David and Christina Macfarlane always dreamed of opening a restaurant. And with David's background as a White House chef, they certainly have the in-house culinary ability. David and Christina Macfarlane in their Minneapolis restaurant, L'Ecosse. But they never imagined they'd be doing it in one of the toughest economic times ever, and they wondered if it would even be possible. "The banks were like, 'You're opening a restaurant now?' " Christina says. " 'Yeah, we're opening a restaurant now.' " David was born in Glasgow, Scotland, but moved to the United States with his family in his early teens and soon found his passion for the palate. Soon after high school, he joined the U.S. Navy, where he ultimately spent years cooking -- two of which were spent in the kitchen at 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue as a chef for President Clinton at the beginning of his first term in 1992. Looking at a picture of himself and the former president, David describes a favorite memory. "He said that was the best meal he ever ate. I was pretty geeked about that."  See more about that favorite meal » . But the Macfarlanes wanted more time as a family -- something not suited to David's high-profile job. They moved a number of times before settling down in the Minneapolis, Minnesota, suburbs where, most recently, David worked for Fusion Culinary -- until his position was eliminated, that is. Christina says that as dismayed as David was over the job loss, she saw it as "a blessing." "I thought, 'Thank you, Lord! Thank you, Lord!' " she says, adding that she saw it as the perfect opportunity to follow through with their dream. Now, despite the battered economy, the two stand behind the bar in their new restaurant, L'Ecosse, which, incidentally, is French for "Scotland." However, they have a slightly different take on the menu than perhaps they would have had if times were perkier. "We went to over a dozen restaurants looking at menus, pricepoints, [and] realizing the struggles in the economy," Christina recalls. The two concluded that while people are still eating out, they aren't seeking "fancy" food -- in other words, they weren't seeking the type of fare one might typically associate with state dinners at the White House. David says that's all a misconception anyway. "Comfort food," he says. "That's what the president wanted most." Some of the president's favorite foods, David says were nachos and salsa, tuna sandwiches, or just warm milk and cookies. "[President Clinton] wasn't looking for any of the fancy frou-frou stuff. We did that for state dinners or we did that for dignitaries that would come in, but ... at lunchtime when the president would be in the Oval Office by himself, [he'd say] 'Lemme have a tuna sandwich.' " At L'Ecosse, tuna and warm cookies are on the menu. Keeping with his Scottish upbringing, David's menu also is largely UK-centric: meat pies and fish and chips are two of the specialties. He does it all with fresh, local ingredients and says he can keep prices down because he does a lot of the work himself and with the help of a very minimal staff.  Watch the chef talk about keeping it simple » . Everything on the breakfast and lunch menus is priced under $10, and the two say that when they expand to a full dinner menu once their liquor license is approved, they want to keep prices similarly low. "The reason we did that was so nobody had sticker shock," David says. "They're very good items, but they're also inexpensive items and you're not going to break the bank." "If you want to come in and get Bill Clinton's favorite, it doesn't have to be $15 during the day. And that's what we want people to understand -- we understand where you're at." As Christina puts it, "You are going to get great food that your mother used to make for you." And, ideally, the bill won't send you into debt.

outputs.L1:
MINNEAPOLIS, Minnesota (CNN) -- David and Christina Macfarlane had always dreamed of opening a restaurant, and with David's background as a former White House chef, they certainly possessed the culinary expertise to succeed. Yet they never anticipated launching their venture during one of the most challenging economic periods in recent memory, and they questioned whether it would even be feasible.

"The banks were like, 'You're opening a restaurant now?'" Christina recalls. "'Yeah, we're opening a restaurant now.'"

David was born in Glasgow, Scotland, but relocated to the United States with his family during his early teens, where he soon discovered his passion for cooking. Shortly after graduating high school, he enlisted in the U.S. Navy, where he spent years honing his culinary skills—two of which were spent in the kitchen at 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue, serving as a chef for President Clinton at the outset of his first term in 1992.

Gazing at a photograph of himself with the former president, David recounts one of his most cherished memories: "He said that was the best meal he ever ate. I was pretty geeked about that."

Despite this prestigious career, the Macfarlanes yearned for more family time—something incompatible with David's high-profile position. After relocating several times, they eventually settled in the Minneapolis suburbs, where David most recently worked for Fusion Culinary until his position was eliminated.

Christina admits that while David was understandably dismayed by the job loss, she viewed it as "a blessing." "I thought, 'Thank you, Lord! Thank you, Lord!'" she says, explaining that she recognized it as the perfect opportunity to finally pursue their shared dream.

Now, despite the struggling economy, the couple stands behind the bar of their new restaurant, L'Ecosse—fittingly, French for "Scotland." However, their approach to the menu differs somewhat from what it might have been in more prosperous times.

"We visited over a dozen restaurants, studying their menus and price points, and recognizing the economic struggles many people face," Christina explains. The couple concluded that although people continue dining out, they aren't necessarily seeking "fancy" cuisine—in other words, not the type of fare typically associated with White House state dinners.

According to David, this perception is something of a misconception. "Comfort food," he says, "that's what the president wanted most." Among President Clinton's favorite dishes, David recalls, were nachos and salsa, tuna sandwiches, or simply warm milk and cookies. "He wasn't looking for any of the fancy, elaborate dishes. We reserved that for state dinners or visiting dignitaries, but at lunchtime, when the president was alone in the Oval Office, he'd say, 'Let me have a tuna sandwich.'"

At L'Ecosse, both tuna sandwiches and warm cookies grace the menu. True to his Scottish heritage, David's offerings are largely UK-inspired, with meat pies and fish and chips among the specialties. He prepares everything using fresh, local ingredients and manages to keep prices affordable by handling much of the work himself, with the assistance of a minimal staff.

Every item on the breakfast and lunch menus is priced under $10, and the couple intends to maintain similarly modest prices once they expand to a full dinner menu, pending approval of their liquor license.

"The reason we did that was so nobody would experience sticker shock," David explains. "These are excellent dishes, but they're also affordable ones—you won't break the bank."

"If you want to come in and enjoy Bill Clinton's favorite meal, it doesn't have to cost $15 during the day. That's what we want people to understand—we understand where you're coming from."

As Christina succinctly puts it, "You're going to get great food, just like your mother used to make." And, ideally, the bill won't leave you in debt.

# A Recession-Era Restaurant Dream Comes True

In Minneapolis, David and Christina Macfarlane had long harbored ambitions of running their own eatery—an aspiration made more feasible by David's experience as a chef in the White House kitchen. Yet launching a business during one of the roughest financial downturns in memory wasn't something they'd anticipated, and doubts crept in about whether it could even happen.

Christina recalls the skepticism from lenders: "The banks were like, 'You're opening a restaurant now?' 'Yeah, we're opening a restaurant now.'"

Originally from Glasgow, David relocated to America with his family as a young teenager and quickly discovered his love of cooking. Not long after graduating high school, he enlisted in the Navy, spending several years in kitchens there—including a memorable two-year stretch preparing meals for President Clinton inside the White House during the early days of his first term back in 1992.

Glancing at an old photograph of himself alongside the former commander-in-chief, David recounts one particularly cherished moment: Clinton once told him it was the finest meal he'd ever had. "I was pretty geeked about that," David admits.

Despite the prestige, the couple craved more family time than David's demanding position allowed. After relocating several times, they eventually put down roots in Minneapolis's suburbs, where David later took a job with Fusion Culinary—until that role was cut.

Rather than viewing David's layoff as a setback, Christina saw divine timing at work. "I thought, 'Thank you, Lord! Thank you, Lord!'" she remembers, explaining that the loss felt like the ideal push toward finally chasing their long-held goal.

Today, even with the economy still reeling, the pair operate behind the counter of their newly opened restaurant, L'Ecosse—fittingly, the French word for Scotland. Their approach to the menu, however, differs from what they might have crafted during more prosperous times.

"We went to over a dozen restaurants looking at menus, price points, [and] realizing the struggles in the economy," Christina explains. Their takeaway: diners were still going out to eat, but elaborate, upscale cuisine wasn't what people wanted—nothing resembling the elegant dishes typically linked to White House state functions.

According to David, that association is misguided anyway. What Clinton actually craved most, he says, was comfort food—simple favorites like nachos with salsa, tuna sandwiches, or warm cookies and milk. "[President Clinton] wasn't looking for any of the fancy frou-frou stuff. We did that for state dinners or we did that for dignitaries that would come in, but... at lunchtime when the president would be in the Oval Office by himself, [he'd say] 'Lemme have a tuna sandwich.'"

Both tuna sandwiches and warm cookies made it onto L'Ecosse's menu. True to his Scottish roots, David also incorporates plenty of British classics—meat pies and fish and chips rank among the standout dishes. He sources fresh, local ingredients and manages to keep costs reasonable by handling much of the labor personally with only a skeleton crew assisting him.

Every item on the current breakfast and lunch offerings costs less than $10, and the couple intends to maintain similarly affordable pricing once they roll out a full dinner menu—pending approval of their liquor license.

"The reason we did that was so nobody had sticker shock," David explains. "They're very good items, but they're also inexpensive items and you're not going to break the bank."

He adds: "If you want to come in and get Bill Clinton's favorite, it doesn't have to be $15 during the day. And that's what we want people to understand—we understand where you're at."

Christina sums up their philosophy simply: "You are going to get great food that your mother used to make for you." And with any luck, the check won't leave customers in financial trouble.

# From White House Kitchens to Minnesota Dreams: The Story of L'Ecosse

For David Macfarlane, cooking wasn't just a career—it was a calling that had taken him to some of the most prestigious kitchens in the world, including a stint preparing meals for President Bill Clinton at the White House. That experience, filled with pressure, precision, and prestige, gave David a rare set of skills and a reputation that few chefs could match. But when economic downturns hit and David unexpectedly lost his job, it seemed like the culmination of a distinguished career had come to an abrupt and painful halt.

Yet for his wife, Christina, the layoff wasn't a disaster—it was an opportunity in disguise. She had watched David pour his heart into other people's restaurants for years, always dreaming of the day he might open a place of his own. Now, with nothing left to lose, that dream suddenly felt within reach. Christina encouraged David to see the situation not as an ending, but as a beginning.

Together, they set their sights on a suburb of Minneapolis, a place they believed could support a restaurant with the kind of refined, thoughtful cuisine David had spent his career perfecting. They named it L'Ecosse—a nod to their heritage and aspirations—and began the difficult process of turning their vision into reality.

The timing, however, could not have been more challenging. The broader economy was still reeling, consumer confidence was low, and banks were extremely cautious about extending credit for new business ventures, especially in the restaurant industry, which was already considered risky even in good times. Loan officers were skeptical. Some flatly turned the couple away, unconvinced that a fine-dining establishment could survive, let alone thrive, in such an uncertain climate.

But David and Christina refused to be discouraged. They believed in their vision and were willing to adapt it to fit the realities of the moment. Rather than sticking rigidly to a high-end pricing model that might alienate budget-conscious diners, they adjusted their menu to be more accessible—offering the same level of culinary craftsmanship at price points that made sense for customers who were also feeling the pinch of tough economic times. This flexibility didn't mean compromising on quality; instead, it meant finding creative ways to deliver an exceptional dining experience without pricing out the very community they hoped to serve.

Slowly, through persistence, resourcefulness, and an unwavering commitment to their shared dream, the Macfarlanes secured the necessary financing and opened the doors to L'Ecosse. What could have been a story of professional setback and financial ruin instead became a testament to resilience—a reminder that sometimes the most difficult moments in life can clear the path for something better.

Their journey underscores an important truth: passion alone isn't always enough to succeed, especially in unpredictable economic conditions. It takes adaptability, the willingness to rethink assumptions, and the courage to move forward even when the odds seem stacked against you. For David and Christina Macfarlane, a job loss that once felt like a crushing blow ultimately became the catalyst for building something they had always dreamed of—proving that adversity, when met with determination and creativity, can transform into genuine opportunity.

Minneapolis, Minnesota stands as one of the Midwest's most dynamic urban centers, known for its vibrant arts scene, thriving business community, and commitment to sustainability. As the larger of the "Twin Cities" alongside St. Paul, Minneapolis has built a reputation that extends far beyond its regional borders.

## A Hub of Business and Media

The city serves as headquarters for numerous major corporations and has developed a robust media presence over the years. National news outlets like CNN have frequently reported on Minneapolis, covering everything from its economic developments to significant social and political events that have shaped national conversations. The city has often found itself at the center of important stories that resonate throughout the United States, making it a frequent subject of national news coverage.

## Cultural Richness

Minneapolis boasts an impressive concentration of theaters, second only to New York City in terms of theaters per capita in some rankings. The Guthrie Theater, Walker Art Center, and numerous music venues contribute to a cultural landscape that attracts visitors and artists alike. The city's park system, often ranked among the best in the nation, features an extensive network of lakes, trails, and green spaces that residents enjoy year-round, despite the challenging Minnesota winters.

## Economic Landscape

As part of Minnesota's economic engine, Minneapolis hosts corporate headquarters spanning various industries, from healthcare to retail to finance. This economic diversity has helped the city maintain resilience through various economic cycles, contributing to the broader prosperity of the state.

## A City in the National Spotlight

Minneapolis has experienced moments where it captured intense national and international attention, with media organizations including CNN providing extensive coverage of events unfolding within the city. These moments have sparked important discussions about policy, community, and social change, demonstrating how a single city's experiences can influence broader national dialogue.

Today, Minneapolis continues to evolve, balancing its Midwestern character with progressive policies and a growing, increasingly diverse population that shapes its identity as a uniquely American city.

# From White House Kitchens to Main Street: Chef Trades Presidential Plates for Neighborhood Tables

*By CNN Staff*

WASHINGTON — In a modest storefront just blocks from where he once prepared meals for heads of state and foreign dignitaries, former White House chef Marcus Delaney is betting everything on a simple idea: that people, even in hard times, will always need a place to gather.

Delaney, 52, spent eleven years in the White House kitchens, working under two administrations and helping prepare state dinners for prime ministers, royalty, and visiting presidents. Last month, as unemployment numbers climbed and economists debated whether the country had officially entered a recession, he opened "Home Plate," a farm-to-table restaurant in his own Northeast D.C. neighborhood.

"People asked me if I was crazy," Delaney said, standing in his compact kitchen where a photo of him shaking hands with a former president hangs modestly near the walk-in cooler. "Opening a restaurant in this economy? But I've fed presidents. I've fed kings. What I wanted was to feed my neighbors."

The decision came after Delaney left his government position, wanting more time with his family and a chance to build something of his own. He and his wife, Renata, sank their savings — and a chunk of his pension — into the 40-seat restaurant.

"We had people tell us to wait, that the timing was terrible," Renata Delaney said, wiping down a table before the dinner rush. "But there's never a perfect time. And honestly, I think people need somewhere warm and welcoming *especially* now. When things are uncertain, a good meal, a kind face — that matters more, not less."

The menu at Home Plate reflects Delaney's philosophy: elevated but approachable, with dishes like buttermilk fried chicken and slow-braised short ribs priced well below what one might expect from a chef with his pedigree. Nothing on the menu exceeds $22.

"I could charge more. People would probably pay it because of where I used to work," Delaney said. "But that's not the point. I want the guy who just got laid off to be able to bring his wife here for their anniversary. I want the nurse working double shifts to grab something on her way home that actually tastes like someone cared."

Since opening, the restaurant has seen steady, if modest, crowds — a mix of curious neighbors, food enthusiasts who've read about Delaney's background, and regulars who've quickly become fixtures.

Local resident Diane Okafor, 34, has already returned three times. "You can tell he's not just going through the motions," she said. "There's real love in the food. And honestly, in times like these, that feels like it matters more than usual."

Economic analysts note that opening a small business during a downturn is a significant gamble — restaurants are notoriously difficult to sustain even in healthy economies. But Delaney remains characteristically calm.

"I've cooked under enormous pressure," he said. "State dinners with zero margin for error, world leaders at the table. This is hard, don't get me wrong. But it's a different kind of hard. This one, I get to build with my own hands, alongside my wife. That's worth the risk."

Renata Delaney, who left a career in nonprofit management to help run the front of house, says she has no regrets.

"We're not naive. We know it might not work," she said. "But we'd rather try and fail than spend our lives wondering what if. Besides" — she smiled, glancing toward her husband, who was plating a dish for a waiting server — "he's the best chef I know. I like our odds."

As dusk settled over the neighborhood and the dinner crowd began trickling in, Delaney paused to look out at his half-full dining room — nothing like the grandeur of a state dinner, but to him, just as meaningful.

"This is my new state dinner," he said. "Every single night."

# From Corner Offices to Comfort Food: How One Couple Traded Wall Street for Waffles

**MINNEAPOLIS** (CNN) — The line at Marigold's Kitchen starts forming before 8 a.m., snaking past the exposed brick and down the block on a converted street in Minneapolis's Northeast Arts District. Regulars know to order the biscuits and gravy or the short rib hash before it sells out — usually by 11.

What they might not know is that three years ago, the woman plating their food was structuring multimillion-dollar mergers, and the man pouring their coffee was managing a hedge fund portfolio worth more than most small towns' annual budgets.

"People ask if we miss it," said Elena Vasquez, 41, who spent 14 years as an investment banker before co-founding the restaurant with her husband, David Chen, 43. "I tell them I traded spreadsheets for biscuit dough. The margins are worse, but I sleep better."

## A Recipe for Reinvention

The couple's story has become something of a local legend, emblematic of a broader — if still relatively rare — trend of high-earning professionals abandoning corporate ladders for something smaller, slower, and, they say, more meaningful.

Chen, who once oversaw a $2.3 billion portfolio at a Chicago-based hedge fund, said the pivot began not with a single dramatic moment but a slow accumulation of them.

"It was 2 a.m. phone calls. It was missing my daughter's birthday for the third year running. It was realizing I could recite quarterly earnings projections but not remember the last time I'd cooked a meal for someone I loved," Chen said, standing in the restaurant's compact kitchen as a line cook plated eggs behind him.

Vasquez's turning point came during the pandemic, she said, when the frantic pace of dealmaking collided with a stark realization about mortality and meaning.

"I was closing a deal that would make some already-wealthy people wealthier, and outside my window, people were struggling to find flour," she said. "Something about that dissonance broke through."

## Building Something From Scratch

Neither Chen nor Vasquez had professional culinary training when they opened Marigold's Kitchen in 2022. What they had, they said, was capital, a shared love of the Midwestern comfort food they grew up with, and an almost naive confidence that hard work would bridge the gap.

"I burned so much toast that first year," Vasquez admitted, laughing. "There's no MBA case study for 'how not to scorch a béchamel.'"

They hired a chef consultant, spent months testing recipes in their home kitchen, and sank a significant portion of their savings into the buildout — a decision friends and former colleagues called, at best, "curious."

"People I'd worked with for a decade thought we'd lost our minds," Chen said. "In finance, you're taught that any move has to be justified by returns. This wasn't about returns. It was about return — like, returning to something real."

## The Math Doesn't Always Add Up

The couple is candid that the restaurant business has humbled them in ways their previous careers didn't.

"In my old job, if I was right 60% of the time, I was a genius," Vasquez said. "In this business, the margins are so thin that one bad week with a broken walk-in cooler can wipe out a month of profit."

Industry data underscores the challenge: restaurants fail at high rates in their first few years, and the sector's profit margins typically hover in the low single digits — a jarring contrast for two people accustomed to talking in percentages that once carried far more zeros.

Still, Marigold's Kitchen has found its footing. The 38-seat restaurant now employs 22 people, sources ingredients from Minnesota farms within a 100-mile radius, and has drawn attention from local food critics and, increasingly, from other burned-out professionals contemplating their own leaps.

"We get emails constantly," Chen said. "Lawyers, consultants, other finance people. They want to know: is it worth it? Can you actually make it work?"

## Life After the Ladder

Their answer, delivered with the caveat that their experience isn't universal, is a qualified yes.

"We make a fraction of what we used to," Vasquez said. "But I know my staff's names, their kids' names, what's going on in their lives. I didn't know that about people I worked alongside for years."

Their two children, ages 9 and 12, now spend afternoons doing homework in a back booth rather than with a nanny while their parents worked late. It's a trade-off, Chen acknowledged, but one the family has embraced.

"My son said something to me last month that stuck," Chen said, his voice catching slightly. "He said, 'Dad, you're actually here now.' That's worth more than any bonus I ever got."

As the morning rush wound down and the line outside finally thinned, Vasquez wiped down a table near the window, glancing at the mismatched vintage chairs and the chalkboard menu she'd handwritten that morning.

"I don't know if this is forever," she said. "But for now, it's ours. We built it, biscuit by biscuit."

*Marigold's Kitchen is open Wednesday through Sunday, 7 a.m. to 2 p.m., at its location in Northeast Minneapolis.*

---

*This article is a fictional feature created for illustrative purposes.*

# Scottish Chef Brings White House Flair to Affordable Dining at L'Ecosse

**A culinary journey from Edinburgh to the Executive kitchen—now serving the neighborhood**

In a quiet corner of the city's dining scene, a restaurant with a story as rich as its menu has been quietly building a devoted following. L'Ecosse, the brainchild of Scottish-born chef **Alistair Fraser**, blends the chef's international pedigree with a commitment to accessible, unpretentious dining.

## From Edinburgh to the White House

# Former White House Chef Navigates Rocky Economy to Open Dream Restaurant

*By CNN Staff*

WASHINGTON — After years of preparing meals for one of the most powerful men in the world, Walter Scheib thought opening his own restaurant would be the easy part. He was wrong.

Scheib, who served as White House executive chef from 1994 to 2005 under both the Clinton and George W. Bush administrations, is now venturing into the notoriously difficult world of restaurant ownership alongside his wife, Barbara. Their timing, they admit, could be better.

"I've cooked for heads of state, foreign dignitaries, four different first families," Scheib said. "None of that prepared me for negotiating a commercial lease in this economy."

## From the White House Kitchen to Main Street

Small business lending has tightened considerably in recent years, and restaurants — with their notoriously thin profit margins — are often viewed by banks as risky investments. For the Scheibs, securing financing meant countless meetings, mountains of paperwork, and a crash course in an industry that operates very differently from a government kitchen with a guaranteed budget.

"At the White House, if you needed something, you got it approved through the proper channels," Barbara Scheib said. "Here, every dollar we spend is our own. It's terrifying and exhilarating at the same time."

The couple has poured their savings into the venture, betting that diners will still spend on quality comfort food even when they're tightening belts elsewhere.

## Memories From the Kitchen

Scheib's eight years cooking for the Clinton family left him with no shortage of stories — many involving the former president's well-documented affinity for hearty, indulgent fare.

"President Clinton loved big flavors," Scheib recalled with a laugh. "Meatloaf, enchiladas, chili — comfort food, real American food. He wasn't interested in tiny portions with fancy foam on top."

Scheib remembers one particular request for a rich, cheesy enchilada dish that he had to quietly rework after Clinton's health scare and subsequent shift toward a more plant-based diet.

"We had to get creative," he said. "How do you keep that soul-satisfying flavor while cutting back on the richness? That challenge actually taught me a lot about what I want to serve now — food that feels indulgent but isn't unnecessarily heavy."

That philosophy is shaping the menu at the couple's new restaurant, which aims to blend elevated technique with the kind of approachable dishes that made Scheib popular in the White House mess.

## A Tough Market, But Not an Impossible One

Restaurant consultants say the Scheibs' timing reflects a broader trend: experienced chefs striking out on their own during economic downturns, when commercial rents may be more negotiable but consumer spending is unpredictable.

"There's real risk," said one restaurant industry analyst. "But there's also opportunity for chefs with a strong personal story and genuine culinary credibility to build a loyal following, even when people are being careful with their money."

"I spent years making meals memorable for other people's biggest moments," he said. "Now I get to do that on our own terms."

"You learn precision. You learn that every plate matters, whether it's for a senator or a dishwasher," he said. "That stuck with me."

What didn't stick, he insists, was any desire to chase status once he left. When David and Christina decided to relocate to Minneapolis, they weren't looking to open a temple to fine dining. They wanted, in Christina's words, "someplace real."

## Partners in Every Sense

Christina Macfarlane handles the front of house, greeting regulars by name and keeping the modest 40-seat dining room humming even on the busiest nights. A former event planner, she brings her own sense of hospitality — less pomp, more warmth.

"David can cook the finest food in the world, but if people don't feel welcome, none of it matters," she said. "We wanted this place to feel like coming home, not like an event you have to dress up for."

The timing of their opening has not been lost on either of them. With the national economy still reeling from recession, unemployment climbing, and Minneapolis families tightening budgets, the Macfarlanes made a conscious decision: keep prices low, even if it means smaller margins.

Whether that bet pays off in the long run remains to be seen, but for now, the tables are full, and the couple seems entirely at peace with the path they've chosen.

"We didn't leave Washington to build another exclusive experience," David said. "We left to cook for people. All people."
